newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Blair shrugs off N.Irish criticism of his marriage.
newsitem.headline: Blair shrugs off N.Irish criticism of his marriage.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair on Thursday shrugged off criticism of his marriage by a Northern Ireland Protestant leader who called him "disloyal" for marrying a Roman Catholic.
Robert Saulters, who was elected head of the Protestant Orange Order on Wednesday, said Blair's marriage to Cherie Booth 16 years ago was "disloyal to one's self, to one's religion".

"I think if he can turn one way, he can turn in the management of the country," Saulters said in a reference to the fact that Blair's Labour Party is well in front in public opinion polls with a general election that must be held in the next five months.

But Blair, a Protestant, dismissed the comments. "I married my wife because I love her. And these religious differences, whether you are a Catholic or a Protestant, I don't think that should matter," he told reporters during a visit to Dublin for a meeting of European socialist leaders.

"What is important is how people are trying to work hard for peace, whichever part of any community they come from," Blair said. "From time to time remarks like this are made but I don't treat them very seriously."
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said Saulters' remarks did not help the cause of peace in Ireland.
"When remarks are being made in relation to Northern Ireland, I would always call for restraint and consideration," he said.
"The effect of remarks like those can be very damaging. They can certainly set back our efforts for peace and reconciliation on this island."
Irish politician Mary Harney, leader of the Progressive Democrats, called Saulters' remarks "the sort of bigotry Northern Ireland could well do without".

The Orange Order is a 200-year-old Protestant organisation with tens of thousands of members, which permeates every level of society in Northern Ireland. It traces its roots to an 18th century victory by Protestant King William of Orange over the invading Catholic monarch James II.
The order holds parades annually which the 40 percent Catholic minority sees as intimidation and a sectarian triumphalism.
